keyIdeas: Every person needs water, food, shelter and energy, and all of them come from natural resources that ecosystems supply.

Total demand on ecosystems depends on two numbers multiplied together: how many people there are and how much each person uses on average (per capita use). Both have climbed sharply over the last 200 years. How much harm that use causes also depends on the technologies people choose, which is where engineering can help.
The lesson sorts human harm to ecosystems into six kinds: over-exploitation, pollution, emerging disease, habitat degradation, invasive species and climate change.
Because the parts of an ecosystem are linked, one human change can set off a chain of effects that loops back to people, like overfishing that let disease-carrying snails multiply.
Engineers judge a solution by its criteria (what success means) and its constraints (limits such as cost and ease of use), and most solutions involve tradeoffs.
A model of a healthy ecosystem gives scientists a target to compare measurements against, so they can tell whether a fix is working and what still needs attention.
Testing and revising is a cycle: monitor, compare, adjust and monitor again. Recovery can be partial, and different parts of an ecosystem can recover at different speeds.
Science can predict the likely results of choices, but people and communities still decide what to do based on their values and needs.

glossary.definition: Per person. To find a per capita amount, divide a group's total (energy used, water used, money earned) by the number of people in the group.
Materials and energy sources from nature that people use, such as water, soil, wood, minerals and fossil fuels.
Benefits that healthy ecosystems give people, such as cleaning water, recycling nutrients, and supplying food and medicines.
Taking fish, trees or other living things from the wild faster than their populations can rebuild, so the populations shrink.
Harmful materials that people add to an ecosystem, such as plastic trash in the ocean or extra nitrogen from sewage.
Able to be broken down over time by natural processes, such as the work of bacteria and fungi. Some products sold as biodegradable break down only under special conditions.
A disease that has only recently started showing up in people, often after people or their animals come into new contact with wild animals that carry it.
Damaging or destroying a natural area so that it can no longer work the way a healthy ecosystem does, such as clearing tropical forest for farmland.
A species that people have moved to a place where it does not naturally live and where it causes harm to the ecosystem or to the economy.
A long-lasting shift in Earth's climate patterns, including changes in average global temperature and in how often severe weather happens.
Oxygen (O₂) dissolved in water, spread out as single molecules among the water molecules rather than as bubbles. Fish, lobsters, oysters and other water animals take in this oxygen to stay alive.
The requirements a design must meet to count as a success, such as lowering snail numbers or protecting a habitat.
The limits a design has to work within, such as cost, materials, time, or how easy it is for people to use.
Giving up some of one good thing to gain more of another, like accepting a smaller coffee harvest in exchange for keeping forest habitat.

explorer.title: More People, More Use Per Person
paragraphs: Brushing your teeth, riding a bus, charging a phone, eating lunch: each one draws on water, fuel, electricity or food, and every one of those resources ultimately comes from Earth's ecosystems.

Across nearly all of the past two thousand years, Earth's population crept upward very slowly. Then it took off: about 1 billion around 1800, 2 billion by 1927, 4 billion by 1974, and 8 billion in 2022.

At the same time, the average person uses more than people used to. Per capita means per person: add up what a whole group uses and divide by the number of people. The lesson's graph shows average energy use per person more than doubling since 1900.

Total demand is roughly population times per capita use, so growth in either one raises the pressure on ecosystems, and growth in both raises it fast. When resources are taken faster than ecosystems can replace them, ecosystems lose some of their ability to provide services such as clean water.

diagram.caption: World population milestones
diagram.alt: Bar chart of world population in billions of people: about 1 billion in 1800, 2 billion in 1927, 4 billion in 1974 and 8 billion in 2022. Each doubling took far less time than the 127 years from 1800 to 1927: the next two doublings took 47 and 48 years.

explorer.watchOut: Fresh water available per person has dropped mostly because a roughly fixed renewable supply is split among more people, not because the rain stopped. Also, the textbook's 'well over 7 billion' is dated: the world passed 8 billion people in November 2022, and the UN reports that growth is now slowing even though the total is still rising.

explorer.title: Six Ways People Disrupt Ecosystems
paragraphs: The lesson sorts the ways humans damage ecosystems into six groups. Naming the problem is the first step toward designing a fix for it.

Over-exploitation means taking living things from the wild faster than their populations can rebuild. Pollution means adding harmful materials, like plastic, to an ecosystem. Habitat degradation means changing or wrecking a natural area so it stops working well, such as clearing forest for farms.

An invasive species is one that people moved to a new place where it does not naturally live and where it causes harm. Asian carp spread because their new home has few predators and plenty of plankton, the same food native fish need. An emerging disease is one that has only recently started infecting people, often after new contact with wild animals. Climate change is a long-term shift in Earth's climate patterns, such as warmer average temperatures, and one of its effects is rising seas.

diagram.caption: The lesson's six disruptions, each with an example and a response
diagram.alt: Table with three columns: disruption, lesson example and one response. Over-exploitation: heavy fishing in Lake Malawi; response: nets with larger holes that spare small snail-eating fish. Pollution: plastic trash in the ocean harming sea turtles; response: reusing, recycling, less packaging and new materials. Emerging disease: Nipah virus passing from fruit bats to pigs to farmworkers; response: keeping farm animals away from bat trees and wearing protective gear. Habitat degradation: tropical forest cleared for sun-grown coffee; response: growing coffee under taller shade trees. Invasive species: Asian carp moving toward the Great Lakes; response: electric barriers in canals. Climate change: rising seas flooding coastal cities such as Miami Beach; response: computer models that guide city planning.

explorer.watchOut: Not every species from somewhere else is invasive. Many crops and garden plants come from other continents but do not spread out of control or cause harm, so the label needs both parts: brought in by people AND harmful. Real problems also often mix several kinds of disruption at once.

explorer.title: Ripples That Come Back to Us
paragraphs: The living and nonliving parts of an ecosystem are linked, so a change in one part can travel a long way. Following a cause-and-effect chain one step at a time helps you predict surprises.

Lake Malawi: as the number of people near the lake grew, fishing increased, including catches of small fish that eat freshwater snails. With fewer snail-eaters, snails multiplied. Those snails can carry parasitic worms that cause bilharzia, so more snails meant more people infected.

Long Island Sound: nitrogen from sewage treatment plants fertilized algae, which grew fast. When the algae died and sank, bacteria broke them down and used up oxygen in the water. Lobsters, fish and oysters could not get enough oxygen, and their numbers fell.

Nipah virus: fruit bats carry the virus. Where pigs were kept under trees in which the bats fed, pigs ate fruit the bats dropped, became infected and passed the virus to the people who worked with them.

Ripples also reach people through ecosystem services, the free benefits healthy ecosystems provide. A coastal marsh soaks up storm floodwater and shelters young fish, so filling one in can mean more flooding and smaller catches. Links can stretch across continents too: warblers that nest in a protected park up north can still decline if the tropical forest where they spend the winter is cleared.

diagram.caption: Three cause-and-effect chains from the lesson (read each row from left to right)
diagram.alt: Table of three chains, each read from the human change to who is harmed. Row 1: heavy fishing in Lake Malawi leads to fewer small snail-eating fish, which leads to more snails carrying parasitic worms, which harms people wading in the lake through the disease bilharzia. Row 2: extra nitrogen from sewage plants makes algae grow fast and then die, bacteria decaying the dead algae use up oxygen, and lobsters, fish and oysters are harmed. Row 3: pigs raised under trees where fruit bats feed eat fruit dropped by infected bats, infected pigs spread the virus, and farmworkers catch Nipah virus.
rows: Bacteria decaying the algae use up oxygen
Pigs raised under fruit-bat feeding trees
Pigs eat fruit dropped by infected bats

explorer.watchOut: The textbook says producers take oxygen out of water during photosynthesis. That is backward: photosynthesis releases oxygen. The big oxygen drain comes from bacteria breaking down huge amounts of dead algae, along with the respiration of living things. Low oxygen collects in bottom water mostly in summer, when a warm surface layer keeps oxygen-rich water from mixing downward.

explorer.title: Judging a Solution: Criteria, Constraints, Tradeoffs
paragraphs: Engineers start by defining the problem. Criteria describe what a successful solution must do. Constraints are the limits it must work within, such as cost, materials, time, or what a community can manage.

At Lake Malawi, a good solution had to cut snail numbers while letting families keep fishing, and it had to be cheap and simple. Nets with larger holes fit those needs: they keep catching bigger fish but let the small snail-eating fish slip through.

Most solutions involve tradeoffs, where gaining one thing means giving up some of another. Coffee grown under taller trees produces fewer beans than coffee grown alone in full sun, but it keeps forest habitat, protects soil and shelters pollinators, and some buyers pay extra for it.

Every solution has limits. Electric barriers in canals are meant to discourage invasive carp from swimming toward Lake Michigan, but no one can be sure yet how well they will keep working. A plastic labeled biodegradable may break down only in special composting facilities, not in the ocean.

diagram.caption: Four solutions from the lesson and the constraint, tradeoff or limit each one faces
diagram.alt: Table with three columns: solution, main criterion, and constraint, tradeoff or limit. Larger-hole fishing nets: protect snail-eating fish and lower snail numbers; must be cheap and easy to use, and fishers catch fewer small fish. Shade-grown coffee: keep forest habitat and its wildlife; fewer beans per farm, often sold at a higher price. Electric barriers in canals: discourage invasive carp from reaching Lake Michigan; not certain to work alone, so used with other controls. Keeping pigs away from bat trees: stop Nipah virus passing from bats to pigs; farms need space away from roosting trees.

explorer.watchOut: 'Biodegradable' does not mean 'safe to toss'. NOAA notes that many plastics labeled biodegradable are not designed to break down quickly in soil, compost piles or seawater, and ordinary plastic breaks into smaller and smaller pieces instead of disappearing.

explorer.title: Test, Compare, Revise
paragraphs: How can you tell whether a huge body of water is healthy? Looking pretty is not enough. Scientists built a model of a healthy Long Island Sound that described normal levels of nonliving parts, like dissolved nitrogen and oxygen, and normal populations of living things.

Measurements from 1987 showed too much nitrogen and too little oxygen across large areas. Because extra nitrogen leads to low oxygen, communities limited the nitrogen that sewage plants released in the 1990s, then kept measuring. Low-oxygen zones shrank, and many fish populations recovered.

The job was not finished. Lobsters did not bounce back as hoped, partly because of things a nitrogen plan cannot control, such as warmer water. So scientists keep monitoring, comparing with the model and adjusting: a cycle of testing and revising.

Models also help with problems still on the way. Climate models give a range of possible sea-level rise, and planners use that range to decide where to protect homes and coastal habitats. Science can predict likely results of choices, but a community still decides what to do.

diagram.caption: Long Island Sound compared with its healthy-ecosystem model
diagram.alt: Table comparing three measurements with the healthy model. Dissolved nitrogen: the healthy model has normal, low levels; in 1987 it was high in large areas; after the nitrogen limits it was lower. Dissolved oxygen: the healthy model has enough for animals; in 1987 it was low in large areas; after the limits the low-oxygen areas were much smaller. Wildlife: the healthy model has healthy native populations; in 1987 lobsters, fish and oysters were reduced; after the limits many fish populations recovered but lobsters stayed below hopes.
rows: Many fish recovered; lobsters still below hopes

explorer.watchOut: A model of a healthy ecosystem is a target for comparison, not a perfect copy of nature. Predictions further into the future come with wider ranges, and recovery can be partial or uneven.

reviewFlags.issue: OCR text is empty or garbled on the image-heavy pages: the p. 386 opener photo has no text, the p. 387 standards box is letter-spaced, and the OCR lost the axes and values of Figure 1 (p. 388), all four Key Science Concept graphs (p. 390), the Figure 6 map labels (p. 395) and the Figure 7 graph (p. 396).
reviewFlags.resolution: All 14 lesson pages were rendered at 110 dpi and read; pp. 390 and 396 were also rendered at 250 dpi and the graphs cropped. Values used in questions (L29-Q01, Q04, Q27) are labeled as approximate readings from the rendered graphs.

evidence.supports: World population stayed nearly flat for most of 2,000 years, then rose steeply after about 1800.

evidence.locator: Key Science Concept graphs (rendered at 250 dpi)
evidence.supports: Per capita energy use rose from about 30 to about 68 gigajoules (1900-2014); fresh water per person fell from about 13,500 to about 6,000 cubic meters (1960-2014).

reviewFlags.issue: p. 398 says producers such as algae 'extract' oxygen from the water during photosynthesis. That is backward: photosynthesis releases oxygen. Low oxygen in nutrient-polluted water comes mainly from bacteria decomposing large amounts of dead algae (plus respiration).
reviewFlags.resolution: The game says algae release oxygen when they photosynthesize and that decomposition of dead algae uses it up. L29-Q11 orders the corrected chain, L29-Q12 repairs the textbook's mistake directly, and the Explorer O3 card's watch-out names it.

evidence.locator: Section 8, Comparing Ecosystem Conditions to the Model
evidence.supports: High nitrogen boosts algae growth; algae decomposition lowers oxygen; low oxygen reduces lobsters, fish and oysters. (Its photosynthesis sentence is the error flagged here.)

evidence.title: How much oxygen comes from the ocean?
evidence.supports: Ocean plankton, including algae, photosynthesize and produce much of the ocean's oxygen.

evidence.title: Indicators: Dissolved Oxygen
evidence.supports: Water bodies receive oxygen from the atmosphere and from aquatic plants; when excess organic material such as large algal blooms is decomposed by microorganisms, dissolved oxygen is consumed.

evidence.title: What is a dead zone?
evidence.supports: Excess nutrients from runoff and wastewater feed algae overgrowth; when the algae die and decompose, the decomposition consumes oxygen.

evidence.title: Hypoxia (ecosystem target indicator)
evidence.supports: Bacterial respiration while decomposing sunken algae is the largest cause of low oxygen in the Sound's bottom water; after nitrogen cuts at wastewater plants, the hypoxic area fell from a 1987-1999 average of 208 square miles to a 2021-2025 average of 83 square miles, about a 60 percent reduction.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 388 says there are 'well over 7 billion people' and predicts 8 billion 'by around 2025'; that is dated, since the UN marked 8 billion on 15 November 2022. The same paragraph says 1927 came '130 years' after 1800, which is a rounded 127.
reviewFlags.resolution: The game uses 8 billion in 2022 with the UN as its source (L29-Q01 graph, Explorer O1 card) and treats the textbook's count as the figure at the time it was written. No question uses the rounded 130.

evidence.supports: About 1 billion people in 1800, 2 billion in 1927 and 4 billion in 1974.

evidence.title: Day of Eight Billion
evidence.supports: The world's population was projected to reach 8 billion people on 15 November 2022.

reviewFlags.issue: On the p. 390 Key Science Concept spread, the panel titled 'Mineral Consumption' actually plots fertilizer use in kilograms per hectare of arable land (a per-area rate, not total mineral use and not per person). The 'Amount of Cultivated Land' axis says 'hectares', but world values of 500-730 must be millions of hectares, and the step near 1991 looks like a change in the data series. The fresh-water caption implies rising consumption causes the per-person drop, but the indicator is a roughly fixed renewable supply divided by population.
reviewFlags.resolution: Questions describe the first graph as fertilizer use per hectare of farmland (L29-Q02, L29-Q04), never quote the cultivated-land values, and teach the fresh-water decline as a division effect (L29-Q05, Explorer O1 watch-out).

evidence.supports: Graph axes: fertilizer consumption (kg/hectare of arable land), land under cultivation (hectares), per capita energy (gigajoules), per capita fresh water (cubic meters).

evidence.title: Fertilizer consumption (kilograms per hectare of arable land): metadata
evidence.supports: This indicator measures plant nutrients from nitrogen, potash and phosphate fertilizers used per unit of arable land.

evidence.title: Renewable internal freshwater resources per capita (cubic meters): metadata
evidence.supports: Renewable internal freshwater per capita is the country's internal renewable river flow and groundwater from rainfall, calculated per person using population estimates.

reviewFlags.issue: Figure 7 (p. 396): the caption says sea level 'may rise another 15 to 65 cm by the year 2050', but the graph's band at 2050 sits at roughly 38-48 cm above its baseline, and both differ from current assessments (NOAA: about 10-12 inches along U.S. coasts between 2020 and 2050). The caption's 'more than 6 cm in the last several decades' understates the roughly 21-24 cm global rise since 1880.
reviewFlags.resolution: No question tests the figure's numbers. L29-Q27 uses only the graph's shape (rising, faster later, a band that widens with time) and its limitations note says the values are dated. The Explorer O5 card speaks of a range of predictions.

evidence.supports: Climate models use past and present data to predict a range of future sea-level rise that planners use to protect coastal communities.

evidence.title: Climate Change: Global Sea Level
evidence.supports: Global average sea level has risen about 21-24 cm since 1880, mainly from melting land ice and thermal expansion of warming seawater; contiguous U.S. coasts are expected to rise 10-12 inches between 2020 and 2050; long-range projections depend mostly on future emissions and on uncertain ice-sheet behavior.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 391 reports that larger-hole nets were adopted at Lake Malawi and that snails and bilharzia infections then declined, but it gives no data. The Stauffer et al. 2006 EcoHealth abstract (opened in review) supports the overfishing chain as correlational evidence: infection in school-aged children was negatively correlated with the density of snail-eating fish, the 1978-1991 rise in infection coincided with a decline in those fish, and at Chembe Village snail-eating fish increased while infection in children declined. The abstract says nothing about net mesh size, so the textbook's 'larger-hole nets reduced bilharzia' outcome remains unverified. The 'Beware Bilharzia' sign in the photo names an association in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe, so the photo probably was not taken at Lake Malawi.
reviewFlags.resolution: Questions test the cause-and-effect logic and the design reasoning the lesson presents (L29-Q09, Q10, Q15, Q19, Q26) and do not assert a measured drop in infections from the nets as fact. L29-Q10 follows the chain 'as the lesson describes it' and cites Stauffer et al. 2006 as correlational support. L29-Q19 and Q26 stay framed as a classroom model and a hypothetical follow-up. The net-size outcome remains unverified.

evidence.supports: Overfishing removed snail-eating fish, snails and parasitic worms increased, and bilharzia rose; low cost and ease of use were constraints; larger-hole nets protect small snail-eating fish.

evidence.title: Schistosomiasis in Lake Malawi: relationship of fish and intermediate host density to prevalence of human infection (Stauffer et al., EcoHealth 3, 2006)
evidence.supports: Infection prevalence was negatively correlated with density of snail-eating fish; where these fish were more abundant snails were fewer; at Chembe Village snail-eating fish increased and schistosomiasis in children declined.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 393 says the Nipah virus spread because communities 'only recently moved into the forest' where the bats live. WHO and CDC describe the 1998-1999 outbreak as starting in pigs on Malaysian pig farms, with fruit bats as the natural host; neither page says communities had just moved into forest.
reviewFlags.resolution: The game describes the bridge the textbook also gives (pigs kept under trees where bats feed) and does not test the 'moved into the forest' claim (L29-Q13). Prevention steps in L29-Q14 match WHO advice. The CDC counts (more than 300 sick, more than 100 died) are consistent with the textbook's 'over 100' and 'more than one-third'.

evidence.supports: Pigs raised under trees where fruit bats roost and feed ate dropped fruit, became infected, and passed the virus to farmworkers; keeping farm animals away from roosting trees and wearing protective gear are recommended.

evidence.title: Nipah virus (fact sheet)
evidence.supports: Fruit bats of the family Pteropodidae are the natural host of Nipah virus; the virus was first identified in 1998 among pig farmers in Malaysia; advice includes protecting pig feed and sheds from bats and wearing gloves and protective clothing when handling sick animals.

evidence.title: About Nipah Virus
evidence.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
evidence.supports: The Malaysia and Singapore outbreak started in pigs and then spread to people; more than 300 people became sick and more than 100 died; Nipah is carried by Pteropus fruit bats.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 395 says people brought Asian carp to the U.S. in the 1970s 'and released them' to eat weeds and snails in lakes and fish farms. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service says silver carp were imported for aquaculture and wastewater ponds to control algae and escaped into the Mississippi River during floods. Federal agencies now use the name 'invasive carp'. The 'Asian carp' group also includes several species with different diets.
reviewFlags.resolution: No question says the carp were released on purpose. Questions describe them only as brought from another continent by people, eating plankton, having few predators and spreading (L29-Q06, L29-Q08, L29-Q31), and use the lesson's name; L29-Q31's limitations note the 'invasive carp' name and the group's mixed diets.

evidence.supports: Asian carp eat large amounts of plankton, have few predators, and electric barriers in Chicago-area canals are hoped to keep them out of Lake Michigan.

evidence.title: Silver carp (Hypophthalmichthys molitrix)
evidence.supports: Silver carp were brought to the United States in the 1970s and 1980s for aquaculture and wastewater treatment as a biological control for algae, escaped into the Mississippi River during floods, and filter-feed on plankton.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 392 says most plastics 'do not break down naturally'. More precisely, they break into smaller and smaller pieces (microplastics) rather than disappearing. The page also presents biodegradable plastic-like materials as a fix, but many products labeled biodegradable break down only in industrial composting facilities. The 2014 Indian Ocean sea-turtle figure ('half of them') comes from a single dated study.
reviewFlags.resolution: L29-Q18 tests evaluating a 'biodegradable' claim, using NOAA's caution. The turtle statistic is not tested. The Explorer O4 watch-out explains fragmentation.

evidence.locator: Section 3, Pollution: Plastics in the Oceans
evidence.supports: Plastics build up in aquatic ecosystems; sea turtles eat or are trapped by them; engineers are developing biodegradable plastic-like materials.

evidence.title: What are microplastics?
evidence.supports: Larger plastic debris degrades into smaller and smaller pieces; microplastics are pieces less than five millimeters long.

evidence.title: Plastic (What is marine debris?)
evidence.supports: Plastic does not break down like other materials; it fragments into smaller pieces that may never fully go away; plastics labeled biodegradable may break down in industrial composting facilities but are not designed to break down quickly in soil, home compost or marine environments.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 394 says 'most coffee agriculture' grows only coffee trees. A 2014 BioScience review reports that many regions are removing shade trees but gives no figure in its abstract showing that most coffee is grown in full sun. Coffee 'trees' are botanically shrubs.
reviewFlags.resolution: No question claims how much coffee is sun-grown. L29-Q17 tests only the sun-versus-shade tradeoff the page describes, L29-Q32 says only that some winter forest is being cleared for coffee, and the game keeps the lesson's word 'trees'.

evidence.supports: Shaded coffee farms yield fewer beans than coffee-only farms but protect forest habitat, soil and pollinators; buyers may pay more for forest-friendly coffee.

evidence.title: Shade Coffee: Update on a Disappearing Refuge for Biodiversity (Jha et al., BioScience 64(5), 2014)
evidence.publisher: Oxford University Press / American Institute of Biological Sciences
evidence.supports: Many coffee-growing regions are removing shade trees from their management; the abstract gives no figure showing that most coffee is grown without shade.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 398 links Long Island Sound's problems to nitrogen pollution and over-exploitation, but the slow lobster recovery also reflects warmer water and other stresses (NOAA Fisheries). The textbook's figures (lobsters doubling by 1997; the status in 2016) are dated.
reviewFlags.resolution: L29-Q23 asks for the most reasonable conclusion: the nitrogen plan helped, but other factors such as warmer water may hold lobsters back. L29-Q22 uses the Long Island Sound Partnership's hypoxia averages. No question uses the 1997 doubling figure.

evidence.locator: Section 8, Using the Model to Restore Ecosystem Health
evidence.supports: After nitrogen limits, low-oxygen areas shrank and many fish recovered, but lobsters had not recovered as much as hoped by 2016.

evidence.title: American Lobster (species directory)
evidence.supports: The Southern New England lobster stock is considered severely depleted; a combination of warmer water, hypoxia and other stresses caused lobster die-offs in western Long Island Sound in 1999 and 2002, and warming may be pushing lobsters offshore and disrupting larval settlement.

evidence.title: Hypoxia (ecosystem target indicator)
evidence.supports: Bacterial respiration while decomposing sunken algae is the largest cause of low oxygen in the Sound's bottom water; after nitrogen cuts at wastewater plants, the hypoxic area fell from a 1987-1999 average of 208 square miles to a 2021-2025 average of 83 square miles, about a 60 percent reduction.

reviewFlags.issue: The words 'criteria' and 'tradeoff' are central to the brief's missions, but the lesson body never uses them: 'criteria' appears only in the p. 387 standards box, and the tradeoff idea is shown on p. 394 without the word. 'Constraints' appears on p. 391 and p. 387.
reviewFlags.resolution: Glossary entries for criteria, constraints and tradeoff use original learner-facing definitions; where each idea appears in the lesson is recorded in this flag rather than in the definitions. Questions define the terms in their prompts (L29-Q15, Q16, Q17).

evidence.locator: Next Generation Science Standards box (ETS1.B, ETS1.C)
evidence.supports: Solutions are evaluated against criteria and constraints, tested and then modified based on test results.
Low cost and ease of use were important constraints for the Lake Malawi communities.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 389 says the night-time satellite image 'shows just how much human populations have changed Earth's ecosystems'. Night lights show where people live and use electricity; they are indirect evidence of human activity, not a direct measurement of ecosystem change.
reviewFlags.resolution: No question treats night lights as a measurement of ecosystem damage. The image is not tested.

evidence.locator: Section 1, night satellite image and caption
evidence.supports: Brightly lit areas mark dense human populations.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 388 says population is still growing at an increasing rate; the UN reports growth is slowing (7 to 8 billion took 12 years, 8 to 9 billion is expected to take about 15 years, to 2037; peak about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s).
reviewFlags.resolution: No question says the growth rate is increasing; L29-Q01 describes the curve only as rising steeply and notes the slowing rate in its limitations. The Explorer O1 watch-out also says growth is slowing while the total still rises.

evidence.supports: The page says the population is continuing to grow at an increasing rate and at a rapid rate; Figure 1 rises steeply after about 1800.

evidence.title: Population (Global Issues)
evidence.supports: Population growth is slowing: going from 7 to 8 billion took 12 years, reaching 9 billion is expected to take about 15 years (to 2037), and population is projected to peak at about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s.

reviewFlags.issue: Two untested figures are dated: p. 397 says more than 23 million people live near Long Island Sound, and p. 389 says a typical person uses more than twice as much energy as someone in the early 1900s. Both are figures at the time the textbook was written.
reviewFlags.resolution: Not tested. Explorer O1 cites only the p. 390 graph's direction of change (per capita energy more than doubling since 1900), and no question or card uses the 23 million count.

evidence.supports: A typical person today uses more than twice as much energy as someone in the early 1900s (as of the textbook's writing).
More than 23 million people live near the sound (as of the textbook's writing).
